why: Getting stuck before writing anything is common and well studied. Soloway's 'rainfall problem' studies found most students could not write a simple averaging program, and the reason was not syntax: beginners lack the small solution patterns (he called them plans) that experienced programmers carry, and the habit of combining them.
So the fix is to learn a small set of patterns on purpose, then practice choosing between them. Solving cold from a blank page before you have the patterns mostly overloads working memory.

methods.name: Worked examples with labelled steps
methods.what: Study a solution split into named steps, saying out loud why each line is there.
methods.evidence: Solid. Labelled worked examples beat solving from scratch for beginners; explaining each step (Chi's self-explanation effect) predicts who learns.

methods.name: Parsons problems
methods.what: Put the given lines of a solution in the right order.
methods.evidence: Solid. Builds the structure with far less memory load than writing from zero.

methods.name: Mixed practice
methods.what: Practice sets where the pattern is not given, so you must choose it.
methods.evidence: Strong in math (72% vs 38% on a later test); not yet tested on coding. It trains exactly the 'which approach?' step.

methods.name: Spaced redoing
methods.what: Redo a problem from a blank file after 1, 3, 7 and 21 days.
methods.evidence: One of the strongest findings in learning science.

start_steps: Say the problem back in your own words: input, output, any limits.
Write two small examples with their correct outputs, one of them an edge case (empty, one item, duplicates).
Solve your examples by hand and write the steps you took in plain English.
Those steps are your plan: paste them in as comments.
Write the simplest correct version first (brute force), even if it is slow.
Turn each comment into code, one at a time.
Run your examples through it, by hand if there is no computer.
Then ask: what is the slow part? Which pattern removes it?
stuck_rule: After 15-20 minutes stuck, look only at the hint or the pattern name, then try again.
Still stuck: study the solution, rewrite it as labelled steps, and mark it 'could not solve' so it comes back tomorrow.
A problem counts as learned only when you solve it cold from a blank file on a later day.
support_stages: Study the worked example and explain each step out loud.
Put its lines in order (the Parsons drill on this page).
Finish a half-written solution: write only the missing step.
Write it with your pattern notes open.
pattern_drill: Once you know a few patterns: read three mixed problems and name the pattern for each within 3 minutes, without coding. The drill on this page does this.

weekly_mix.why: In most data engineering loops; window functions, joins, deduplication.
Rarer for data roles, but Amazon, Meta and software or ML roles still run them.

daily_plan: 5 minutes: redo the problems that are due.
30-40 minutes: one pattern at its current stage.
10 minutes: explain one solution out loud as if to an interviewer.
in_the_interview: Think out loud from the first minute; silence is what makes it look like you are stuck.
Ask about input size, empty input, duplicates and what to return when nothing is found.
Say the brute-force idea and its cost before optimising.
If you are stuck for a few minutes, say what you have tried and ask for a hint; that is normal and scored better than a long silence.
Test with your examples before saying you are done.
Some companies now run AI-assisted coding rounds: explain what you asked the tool for and how you checked its output.

two_week_start.do: Hash map: worked example, Parsons drill, then Two Sum and Valid Anagram. SQL: Duplicate Emails.
Redo Day 1 problems cold. Two pointers: worked example, Parsons, Valid Palindrome. SQL: Combine Two Tables.
Sliding window: worked example, Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock. SQL: Customers Who Never Order.
Redo due problems. Stack: Valid Parentheses. Python data: group and aggregate example.
Binary search: Binary Search. SQL: Rising Temperature. Python data: dedupe-latest example.
Pattern drill (name the pattern) for 10 minutes, then redo everything marked shaky.
Rest, or one timed mixed problem explained out loud.
Redo due problems. Prefix sums: Subarray Sum Equals K. SQL: Second Highest Salary.
Intervals: Merge Intervals. SQL: Rank Scores. Python data: compare with the previous row.
Heap: Kth Largest Element. SQL: Game Play Analysis IV. Python data: sessions.
Graph search: Number of Islands. Python data: parse and clean logs.
Topological sort: Course Schedule. SQL: Department Top Three Salaries.
Pattern drill, then two mixed problems timed at 25 minutes each, talking out loud.
Redo everything due. Pick the weakest pattern for next week.

patterns.name: Hash map: remember what you have seen
patterns.clue: Find a pair, a duplicate, a count, or whether two things contain the same items.
patterns.idea: Walk the data once and keep a dict of what you have seen, so each lookup is O(1) instead of a second loop.

steps: Make a dict that maps each value to where you saw it.
Walk the list once.
Work out the partner this value needs and check whether you have already seen it.
Not found yet: store this value so a later one can find it.

patterns.name: Two pointers
patterns.clue: A sorted array, a pair or triple with a target sum, a palindrome, or changing an array in place.
patterns.idea: Start one pointer at each end (or both at the start) and move the one that brings you closer to the goal.
patterns.cost: O(n) time, O(1) memory (plus the sort if the input is not sorted).

steps: Put one pointer at each end.
Keep going until they meet.
Skip characters that do not count (spaces, punctuation).
Compare the two ends; a mismatch means it is not a palindrome.
Both match: move both inward.

check.call: is_palindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama')

patterns.name: Sliding window
patterns.clue: The longest or shortest contiguous substring or subarray that meets a rule.
patterns.idea: Keep a window [left, right]. Grow it by moving right; when the rule breaks, shrink it by moving left. Record the best window as you go.
patterns.cost: O(n) time: each element enters and leaves the window once.

lines.code: if ch in last_seen and last_seen[ch] >= left:

steps: Track where each character was last seen.
Start an empty window and a best score.
Grow the window one character at a time.
The rule breaks (a repeat inside the window): move left past the earlier copy.
Record this character's position.
Keep the best window length.

patterns.name: Prefix sums
patterns.clue: Sums over ranges, or how many subarrays add up to a value.
patterns.idea: Keep a running total. The sum of a range is one running total minus an earlier one, so you can look earlier totals up in a dict.

steps: Set up a counter, a running total, and a dict of earlier totals (the empty start counts once).
Add each number to the running total.
A stretch ending here sums to k when an earlier total equals running - k: add how many there were.
Record this running total for later positions.

patterns.name: Sort, then sweep (intervals)
patterns.clue: Meetings, time ranges, overlaps, or anything with a start and an end.
patterns.idea: Sort by start time, then walk once, comparing each interval with the last one you kept.
patterns.cost: O(n log n) for the sort, then O(n).

steps: Sort by start so overlaps sit next to each other.
Walk the sorted list.
Overlaps the last kept interval: stretch its end.
No overlap: keep it as a new interval.

patterns.name: Stack
patterns.clue: Matching brackets, undo, nested structure, or 'the next bigger value'.
patterns.idea: Push things you will need to come back to; pop when the matching or closing item arrives.

lines.code: if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:

steps: Map each closing bracket to its opening one.
Start an empty stack.
Read one character at a time.
A closing bracket must match the most recent opening one.
An opening bracket waits on the stack.
Valid only if nothing is left open.

patterns.name: Binary search
patterns.clue: Sorted data, 'find the smallest value that works', or a hint that O(log n) is expected.
patterns.idea: Look at the middle, throw away the half that cannot hold the answer, repeat.

steps: Set the search range to the whole list.
Keep going while the range is not empty.
Look at the middle.
Found it.
Throw away the half that cannot contain the target.
Not there.

patterns.name: Heap (top k)
patterns.clue: The k largest, smallest, closest or most frequent items.
patterns.idea: Keep a heap of size k; push each item and pop the smallest when it grows past k. What remains is the top k.

steps: Start an empty min-heap.
Add each number.
Too many: drop the smallest, so only the k largest stay.
The smallest of the k largest is the answer.

patterns.name: Grid and graph search (DFS/BFS)
patterns.clue: Connected areas, islands, spreading, or the fewest steps from A to B.
patterns.idea: From each unvisited start, visit everything reachable and mark it. DFS for 'how many areas', BFS for 'fewest steps'.
patterns.cost: O(rows x cols) or O(nodes + edges).

lines.code: if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= rows or c >= cols or grid[r][c] != "1":

steps: Note the grid size.
Define a visit that stops at the edge or at water.
Mark the cell visited (sink it), then visit its four neighbours.
Scan every cell; each unvisited land cell starts a new island.
Return the island count.

patterns.name: Topological sort (dependencies)
patterns.clue: Prerequisites, build order, task scheduling, or 'can all of these finish?'.
patterns.idea: Count what each task still waits for. Start with tasks that wait for nothing; finishing one frees the tasks that depended on it. The same idea runs an Airflow DAG.

lines.code: ready = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if waiting_on[i] == 0)

steps: Count what each course waits for and what it unlocks.
Fill both from the prerequisite pairs.
Courses waiting for nothing are ready.
Take a ready course and count it done.
It frees its dependents; any that now wait for nothing become ready.
Everything finished only if there was no cycle.

patterns.name: Linked list pointers
patterns.clue: Reverse, merge or find a cycle in a chain of nodes.
patterns.idea: Keep the few pointers you need (previous, current, next) and update them in the right order so nothing is lost.

steps: Nothing comes before the first node yet.
Walk the chain.
Save the next node before you change anything.
Point this node backwards.
Step both pointers forward.
The old tail is the new head.

patterns.idea: Answer for an empty tree first, then build each node's answer from its left and right answers.

steps: An empty tree has depth 0 (the stopping case).
A node's depth is one more than its deeper side.

patterns.name: Dynamic programming (choices that build on earlier answers)
patterns.clue: Count the ways, the minimum cost, or the best total when each step is a choice.
patterns.idea: Name the state (the best answer up to here), write how it comes from the previous states, then fill it in order.
patterns.cost: Usually O(n) or O(n x m).

lines.code: take, skip = skip + x, max(take, skip)

steps: The state: best total if this house is robbed (take) or not (skip).
Go house by house.
Taking this house means skipping the last; skipping it keeps the better of both.
The answer is the better final state.

patterns.name: Backtracking (try, then undo)
patterns.clue: List every subset, ordering or combination.
patterns.idea: Make a choice, explore everything after it, undo the choice, and try the next one.
patterns.cost: Exponential, so it is used when the answer itself is every option.

steps: Collect results and the current choice.
At the end of the list, save a copy of the choice.
Choose this item and explore the rest.
Undo it and explore the rest without it.
Start from the first item.

patterns.name: Group and aggregate
patterns.clue: Totals, counts or averages per customer, day, region or any key.
patterns.idea: One pass with a dict keyed by the group (or GROUP BY). Decide up front what to do with missing values.

steps: Start a total per key that defaults to 0.
Read each row.
Skip rows with no amount (say so in the interview).
Add the amount to its customer's total.
Return plain totals.

sql.query:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE amount IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 5
ORDER BY customer_id
setup: CREATE TABLE orders (customer_id TEXT, amount REAL)

patterns.name: Deduplicate, keep the latest
patterns.clue: Repeated records, change logs, 'current state' of each id, idempotent loads.
patterns.idea: Key by the id and keep the row with the newest timestamp (or ROW_NUMBER() = 1 in SQL).

lines.code: if key not in latest or rec["updated_at"] > latest[key]["updated_at"]:

steps: Keep the newest row seen for each id.
Read each record.
Replace the kept row when this one is newer.
Return one row per id.

sql.query:
SELECT id, v FROM (
    SELECT id, v, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
    FROM events
) AS ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY id
setup: CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER, updated_at INTEGER, v TEXT)

patterns.name: Top N per group
patterns.clue: The top 3 salaries per department, the latest 5 orders per customer, the second highest of anything.
patterns.idea: Rank inside each group (DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER over a partition), then filter by rank. In Python, a heap per group.

lines.code: return {dept: heapq.nlargest(n, salaries) for dept, salaries in sorted(groups.items())}

steps: Collect the values for each group.
Put each row in its group.
Keep the n largest in each group.

sql.query:
SELECT dept, salary FROM (
    SELECT dept, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employees
) AS ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC
setup: CREATE TABLE employees (dept TEXT, salary INTEGER)

patterns.name: Compare with the previous row
patterns.clue: Day-over-day change, 'higher than yesterday', consecutive values, churn between periods.
patterns.idea: Sort by time, then look at each row next to the one before it (LAG in SQL, zip(rows, rows[1:]) in Python).
patterns.cost: O(n log n) for the sort.

lines.code: for prev, cur in zip(readings, readings[1:]):
if cur["day"] - prev["day"] == 1 and cur["temp"] > prev["temp"]:

steps: Sort by time so neighbours are next to each other.
Pair each row with the one before it.
Count it only when the days are consecutive and the value rose.

sql.query:
SELECT day FROM (
    SELECT day, temp, LAG(temp) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_temp, LAG(day) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day
    FROM weather
) AS w
WHERE day - prev_day = 1 AND temp > prev_temp
setup: CREATE TABLE weather (day INTEGER, temp INTEGER)

patterns.name: Sessions and streaks (gaps and islands)
patterns.clue: Group events into sessions, find streaks, or split a timeline wherever there is a gap.
patterns.idea: Sort by time; start a new group whenever the gap from the previous event is too big. In SQL: flag the starts with LAG, then a running SUM of the flags numbers the groups.

lines.code: if sessions and t - sessions[-1][-1] <= gap:

steps: Start with no sessions.
Walk the events in time order.
Close enough to the last event: same session.
Too far: start a new session.

sql.query:
SELECT user_id, SUM(is_start) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY t) AS session_no, t
FROM (
    SELECT user_id, t,
           CASE WHEN t - LAG(t) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY t) <= 30 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_start
    FROM clicks
) AS flagged
ORDER BY user_id, t
setup: CREATE TABLE clicks (user_id TEXT, t INTEGER)

patterns.name: Parse and clean
patterns.clue: Log lines, CSV or JSON with bad rows, mixed formats, 'count errors per hour'.
patterns.idea: Define what a valid record looks like, parse each one, count (never silently drop) the bad ones, then aggregate.

steps: Write the shape of a valid line as a pattern.
Set up the counts and a bad-row counter.
Parse each line.
Count lines that do not parse instead of dropping them silently.
Pull out the fields.
Count errors per date and hour.
Return both, so bad data is visible.

patterns.name: Joins and anti-joins
patterns.clue: Combine two sources, 'customers who never ordered', 'employees who earn more than their manager'.
patterns.idea: Build a lookup (set or dict) from one side, then walk the other. In SQL: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL for 'never'.

lines.code: return [c["name"] for c in customers if c["id"] not in ordered]

steps: Build a set of everyone who ordered.
Keep the customers who are not in it.

sql.query:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL
setup: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER, name TEXT)

patterns.name: Large files with generators
patterns.clue: 'The file does not fit in memory', streaming rows, chunked processing.
patterns.idea: Yield one record at a time instead of building a list, so memory stays flat however big the file is.

steps: Read rows lazily from the open file.
Hand back each valid row one at a time (yield, not a list).
Consume the stream without ever holding it all.

patterns.name: Running totals and moving averages
patterns.clue: Cumulative sums, 7-day averages, rolling metrics.
patterns.idea: Keep a window of recent values and its sum; add the new value, drop the oldest. In SQL: a window frame (ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).

steps: Keep the recent values, their sum, and the output.
Add each new value to the window and the sum.
Window too long: drop the oldest from both.
Record the average of what is in the window.

sql.query:
SELECT day, AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_2
FROM sales
ORDER BY day
setup: CREATE TABLE sales (day INTEGER, amount REAL)
